open-question.question: Six of prompt 1's and three of prompt 2's deliberately-left-open items (team names, undoing an award, skipping a question, progress shown, keyboard control, reload survival; the built-in questions surviving, choosing a set at the start, answer validation) also appear as scored implied-requirement lines, so a minimal choice the prompt leaves open loses points on the implied axis. Where an item appears in both lists, which list keeps it: is it a scored implied line, an unscored open decision, or both with the overlap stated as intended?

The assess delivery differs from every manual delivery in two things at once, Cairn's structure and a planned stakeholder turn, and no manual delivery gets a planned turn, so the assess gain over manual cannot be attributed to Cairn alone. Does the benchmark add a manual delivery with a planned turn (the model lists the questions it needs answered, the operator answers them under the same disclosure rule, then the build instruction follows), and if so is it a primary delivery with a README row or an analysis-only control?

The operator discloses a hidden requirement in reply to any question whose answer the statement changes, which a catch-all such as "anything else I should know before I start?" satisfies, so the hidden axis can reward a vague closing question rather than a surfaced one. What test decides that a question bears on a hidden requirement?

After each invocation the harness hands the final message to the operator; a message that asks gets a reply while one that reports completion, a stop, or an error, or closes with an offer, gets none, but nothing says who makes that classification, and it is not recorded. How is the reply-or-no-reply classification of a final message made and recorded?
open-question.alternative: Every final message, a resumed session's included, goes to the operator itself, whose guideline states the reply rule; its output is either a reply or one fixed no-reply line carrying a one-clause reason. No harness rule runs first. Every such call writes its record file, the no-reply ones included, with the closing line stating the verdict and the reason. A no-reply verdict is not an operator turn: it adds no attentive session and no reply to the cap, and its tokens join the operator's own figures, kept apart from the scenario's totals. Needs no new component or versioned input: the one model already defined as the stakeholder makes the judgment a stakeholder would make, under the operator definition the manifest already pins, and every verdict lands in the record file the draft already keeps. The judge holds the hidden knowledge, so a borderline closing offer may be read as a question it can answer, which ties the hidden axis to how the operator reads ambiguity rather than to what the session asked; it also costs one operator call per invocation, about a dozen per cairn chain against one per manual run.

The harness first matches each final message against Cairn's fixed success, no-op, and stop lines, and a match is a no-reply verdict with no model call, recorded as the matched line; every other message goes to the operator, which replies or outputs the fixed no-reply line with a one-clause reason, as in the operator-classifies option. Every verdict, matched or judged, is written to the invocation's record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn, adds no attentive session, and the operator's tokens stay apart from the totals. A cairn chain's ordinary invocations are classified deterministically and for free, so model judgment and the operator's cost are spent only on messages that are genuinely open, which is every manual run's final message and any cairn message outside the fixed set. Viable only as far as Cairn fixes the wording of its no-op and stop lines, an axis the fixed-stop-line question owns; the two families are classified by different means, a cairn message by rule and a manual one by judgment, and the judged path still lets the holder of the hidden knowledge decide.

A distinct model call, with no tools and a fixed model and effort pair, defined and versioned with the operator definition and recorded in the manifest, reads only the final message under a stated rule (asks, confirms, or offers a choice: reply; reports completion, a stop, or an error, or closes with an offer: no reply) and outputs the verdict and a one-clause reason. It never sees the prompt or the hidden knowledge. Only a reply verdict invokes the operator. Every verdict and reason goes into the invocation's record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn and adds no attentive session; the classifier's tokens are recorded beside the operator's, apart from the totals. The judgment is made blind to the hidden knowledge and to the prompt, so whether a session receives a reply depends on what its message says alone, never on whether the stakeholder holds something it could disclose. Adds a second model input to version, pin, and keep identical across a comparison set, plus a call on every invocation of every scenario, and its stated rule still has to settle the offer-closing-with-a-question case the draft leaves fuzzy.

The harness first matches each final message against Cairn's fixed success, no-op, and stop lines, a match being a no-reply verdict with no model call; every other message goes to the separate blind classifier of the separate-classifier option, which outputs the verdict and a one-clause reason, and only a reply verdict invokes the operator. Every verdict, matched or judged, is written to the record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn and adds no attentive session; classifier tokens stay apart from the totals. Combines the deterministic, cost-free handling of every fixed Cairn line with a judgment that never sees the hidden knowledge, so the only model-classified messages are the open ones and their classification cannot lean toward disclosure. The most moving parts: a line table that must track Cairn's fixed wording, an axis the fixed-stop-line question owns, plus a second versioned model input; cairn and manual messages are still classified by different means.

No model classifies. The harness applies one stated textual rule to every final message: a message matching one of Cairn's fixed status or stop lines gets no reply, and any other message gets a reply exactly when its last paragraph ends in a question mark. The verdict and the rule clause that produced it are written to the invocation's record file; a no-reply verdict is not an operator turn and adds no attentive session. Fully reproducible and free: the same message always gets the same verdict on any machine and under any operator version, so the classification adds no noise of its own to the hidden axis or the attentive-session count. A textual rule misreads exactly the case the question is about: an offer phrased as a question ("Want me to add tests?") gets a reply and a request phrased as a statement ("Let me know which you prefer.") gets none, so manual runs' route to the hidden knowledge turns on punctuation; it also depends on the fixed-line wording the fixed-stop-line question owns.

The draft keeps the reply rule as written, naming no classifier and recording no verdict; the gap is rejected in the text with the reason that the classification is a harness implementation detail, and the record files stay one per operator turn, so a no-reply message leaves no trace beyond the invocation output. Adds nothing to the design or to a run's cost and leaves the harness's author free to choose the mechanism when the harness is built. Whether a session receives a reply, and with it a manual run's only route to the hidden knowledge, stays an unstated and unrecorded judgment that can differ between implementations and runs, so a hidden-axis difference cannot be traced to it after the fact.

open-question.question: Every invocation loads the user-level configuration beside the plugin under test (other plugins, MCP servers, hooks, settings); the pre-flight checks only that Cairn is not installed at user level, and the manifest's user_config digests can detect a change but cannot recreate the configuration on another machine. How is the host configuration a run executes under isolated from the maintainer's own and made reproducible?

Both Cairn agents and every manual invocation run with web search and fetch enabled, and once the Pages site and the run branches are public a web search for the project's name finds earlier artifacts and the repository holding the hidden requirements. Are web search and fetch tools disallowed in scenario invocations?

From its clone an agent can read the benchmark checkout, whose inputs area holds the hidden-requirement statements, the sibling clones in the shared scratch directory, and other runs' session transcripts under the host's projects directory, and the maintainer's notes record that Docker Desktop blocks these runs on the development machine. What confinement keeps a run from reading the benchmark checkout, other clones, and other runs' transcripts, and on what machine do runs then execute?

Nothing states what OS, tools on PATH, and browsers a run finds, though these shape what every scenario can build and what the rater can drive. Is the execution environment declared as a versioned shared input of a comparison set, recorded in the manifest only, or left unrecorded?
open-question.alternative: The run environment (OS and version, the tools on PATH with their versions, the installed browsers) is written as one environment definition under the inputs area, versioned by content under an id like the operator definition, and listed among the shared inputs; the pre-flight probes the live machine and refuses the run when it does not match the definition, the manifest records the definition's id, and a change to the definition starts a new comparison set. The run agent is told nothing beyond what the seed's CLAUDE.md already says, and the rater's browser stays in the rater definition as now. Puts the environment under the same rule as every other input that shapes results (byte-identical across scenarios, recorded by content, a change never mixed into a comparison), and gives a later re-run on another machine a target it can be checked against rather than a guess. Every probed version has to be held still for a whole campaign, so auto-updating browsers and tools must be pinned or disabled and a drifted machine refuses runs until reprovisioned; whether the pin can be enforced depends on the machine and confinement the filesystem-reach question settles, and whether a change starts a new set rests on the axis the comparison-set-definition question owns.

The environment is declared inside the seed's CLAUDE.md, which the draft already calls an environment description: it names the OS, the tools on PATH, and the browsers a run finds, so the seed tag versions the declaration and no separate input or manifest field is added; the pre-flight probes the machine against the same list and refuses on a mismatch, and a change to the environment is a change to the seed and starts a new comparison set through the seed tag. The run agent reads the declaration; the rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Adds no new kind of input and no new versioning path, and every scenario learns equally what it can use (for example that no package manager is present), so no run spends turns discovering the machine or builds against a tool that is absent. Any environment change, even a browser patch release, bumps the seed tag, which invalidates every phase-1 run as a parent for phase 2 and moves the trend's seed line; and telling the agent which tools exist shapes what each scenario builds, turning a measurement condition into part of the prompt every run reads.

The environment is declared as an environment definition under the inputs area, as a provisioning target rather than a set-defining input; the harness probes the live machine at the manifest step and records the observed OS, PATH tool versions, and browsers in an environment field of the manifest beside the definition's id, and a mismatch with the definition is flagged by the analysis step and reported beside the affected rows rather than refusing the run or starting a new comparison set. The run agent is told nothing new; the rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Gives another machine a stated target to reproduce while letting a campaign that spans days absorb a browser or tool auto-update without discarding the set, with every deviation visible in the record instead of hidden. A flagged mismatch still sits inside one comparison, so a difference between scenarios can be partly the environment's, against the rule that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions; the analysis must decide per flag whether it matters, which is a judgment the rest of the design avoids. Whether drift may stay inside a set is the axis the comparison-set-definition question owns.

No environment is declared. The harness probes the live machine at the manifest step and records what it finds (OS and version, a fixed list of tools on PATH with their versions, installed browsers) in an environment field of each run's manifest; the environment is not a shared input, a change starts no new comparison set, and the analysis may group or compare runs by the recorded values after the fact. The rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Costs one probe and one manifest field, needs no provisioning or pinning, and still leaves a record from which any later question about what a run found can be answered. Records without controlling: runs on two machines or across an update mix silently within a set unless someone reads the field, a later re-run has nothing to reproduce but a list of observed versions, and the fixed probe list misses any tool a run reached that the list did not name.

The environment is neither declared nor recorded: a run finds whatever the machine running the harness has, and the draft states this choice with its reason (all scenarios of a campaign run on one machine, so the environment is common to them) instead of leaving it unsaid. Nothing to build, pin, or maintain, and within one campaign on one unchanged machine every scenario does meet the same environment. Results cannot be reproduced or audited elsewhere, and a tool or browser update during a campaign, or a move to another machine (which the filesystem-reach question may require), changes what scenarios can build with no trace, mixed into the trend as if it were a plugin change.

open-question.question: A Cairn skill that stops on its own precondition prints a message and exits 0, so the harness, which stops the chain only on a non-zero exit, carries on past it and can record a chain that closed an empty milestone as every invocation made. By what signal does the harness detect that an invocation stopped on a skill's own check rather than completing?

Each skill's success line is fixed and identifier-free, but apart from the bootstrap's no-op line the no-op and precondition-stop messages are prose whose wording the files only exemplify, so a harness matching final messages can recognize success but not which stop occurred. Does Cairn fix the wording of every skill's no-op and stop lines in this milestone?

finish-current-milestone closes a milestone whenever TASKS_TODO.md holds no section, so a chain whose derivation line refused to run finishes an empty milestone, clears the pointer, and leaves a tree that looks like a completed chain. Should the finish skill refuse to close a milestone that recorded no completed task?

An early stop is counted as a result, which also covers a usage limit, an API overload, or a network error reaching an invocation as a failed call, and Cairn spends the most tokens so is the likeliest to hit them. What does the harness do with an invocation that ends in an infrastructure failure rather than in the model's own stop?

No scenario invocation carries a time or turn limit while the rater has one, so a runaway session can hold a run open indefinitely. Does each invocation get a time or turn limit, and how is an invocation that hits it classified?

A new rating writes new browser tests for every checklist line, so two ratings of one artifact can test the same line at different strictness, and the draft's claim that a second rating gets the same number holds only for re-running an existing test. What must a rater version pass before it may rate a comparison set, and what is the acceptance rule?

The lost count compares two independent ratings, the parent's and the child's, so rater noise shows as lines lost or gained when nothing changed, and no agreement figure is reported anywhere. Is a sample of each comparison set's artifacts rated twice with the agreement reported beside the scores, and at what sample size?

Each checklist line names a behaviour and nothing more, so a weak test (an undo button exists) and a strict one (the award is actually reversed) both satisfy it. Does each line carry a short specification of the case its test must drive and what it must assert?

A test line the rater could not drive the artifact to scores zero like a missing behaviour, with the not-proved count reported beside the axis, which penalises an artifact a browser test finds hard to drive (a canvas-based UI) regardless of what a host could do with it. How is a not-proved line scored?

The rater receives the entry file and the files it loads, so an editor page reached only by a link or a saved set file beside the HTML never reaches it and every line about it fails as not proved. What part of a run's tree does the rater receive?

The run script detects a root index.html, and a run that put its entry elsewhere gets the manifest's entry field by hand, against the rule that nothing about a run is done by hand and by a person who sees the manifest's scenario. How is a run's entry point determined when it is not a root index.html?

The reference strategy models_strategy_1 is said to be written from Cairn's own usage snippets, but only three of its twelve rows match docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, which assigns Opus at high to the bootstrap, define, goto, and finish lines, Fable at high to the starting-state, review, recommend, and derive lines, and Opus at xhigh to task completion. Which of the two changes to match the other, or do they diverge with the "as it is used" claim dropped?

docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md repeats the review pass until it reports convergence, raises the review line to a stronger model for a stuck milestone, and re-runs task completion after a usage-limit stop, none of which a fixed message list can express, and the YOLO chain runs the review once. Does the delivery model gain a bounded loop (a named span of lines repeated up to a declared count until the review line prints its convergence verdict), with the bound part of the delivery?

The define line records "Carry out the task described in PROJECT.md." verbatim as milestone 1's goal, and phase 2 overwrites that file, so from then on the recorded goal points at prompt 2 and the phase-2 starting-state pass reads a milestone whose goal no longer describes what it built. What text does the define line carry as the milestone goal?

Phase 1 is run for every scenario "as many times as the set calls for", with no number set and no stopping rule, so a margin between two scenarios can be noise. How many runs per scenario does a comparison set require?

The ranking table has a runs column but no spread or interval beside any score, so a reader cannot tell a margin between two scenarios from noise. Is a per-run spread or interval reported beside every score, and where?

The rank orders scenarios by overall score and breaks ties by cost, with no threshold below which two scores count as equal, so a difference within noise still orders two rows. Is there a margin under which two overall scores tie and cost decides?

Each family's radar curve is drawn from its highest-ranked scenario, and the best of several noisy scores is biased upward, more so for Cairn, which has many configurations (versions times strategies) where manual has few. Which scenario is each family's radar curve drawn from?

The hidden-requirements axis rests on two checks per run (one reading line in phase 1 and one test line in phase 2) yet weighs one third of the overall score, as much as roughly thirty-seven implied lines. Does the hidden axis keep equal weight in the overall score, or is it reported beside an overall computed without it?

A comparison set is one seed tag and one version of each prompt, yet an operator change must also start a new set, the analysis groups by rater version, and the host CLI auto-updates across a campaign that spans several days. Which versions define a comparison set?

Nothing lists which scenarios a comparison set must contain, so "complete" is undefined and the strongest manual strategy can be left out while the radar claims to compare against it. Does a comparison set declare a roster of scenarios that must all be rated before it counts as complete, and what must the roster hold?

The published trend follows per-scenario aggregates across comparison sets and plugin commits, so a change to the inputs and a change to the plugin are mixed in one line, against the rule that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions. How does the trend continue when a shared input changes?

Phase 2 starts as soon as the parent's Run: commit exists, which implies runs in parallel, yet every run's pre-flight requires the benchmark checkout to be on a clean main and every run commits to it. Are runs sequential, or how do concurrent runs share the benchmark checkout?

Each hidden requirement's evidence must settle the question once asked while the prompt alone gives no reason to ask, and nothing has tested this: prompt 1's "ten questions of its own" may already invite the topic question, and prompt 2's "keep them for the next party" sits close to the export convention. What procedure and acceptance rule calibrate each prompt's hidden requirement before scored runs?

The animal reading line scores the count of animal questions out of ten, which is undefined for an artifact that holds more than ten questions or draws ten per game. How is that line scored for such an artifact?

"About an animal" has borderline items, such as the zoo's visitor count or how many animals live at the zoo, while a reading line promises one defensible answer per item. Does the hidden-requirement entry state a classification rule for borderline items?

The benchmark's main branch is public, so the hidden requirements, the operator records, and every artifact are public and future models will train on them, wearing down the no-canned-solution requirement over time. How does the benchmark limit or account for its inputs and results leaking into training data?

Each prompt's checklist is derived from the draft's project section, which no version pins, and nothing freezes the checklist and hidden requirements before a comparison set's first scored run. Are the checklist and hidden-requirement entries frozen before the first scored run of a set, and how?

The README shows only the latest complete comparison set, so a seed bump replaces a bad result on the landing page with no trace. Does the page keep superseded comparison sets linked with the reason each was superseded?

The operator's input is the prompt text as committed, which in phase 2 is prompt 2 alone, so a phase-2 question about the game's existing flow reaches a stakeholder who does not know the game they asked for in phase 1. Which prompts does the operator receive in phase n?

The ranking-table section opens by saying the table shows that Cairn beats the other approaches, while the radar text says the page states no claim the data does not. Does that sentence change to say the table shows whether Cairn beats them?

Every gap in ideas/benchmark_design_gaps.md is to end as a decision in the draft, and the report's Where references are line numbers that shift with every edit of the draft. What happens to the report once its gaps are resolved?

The draft's examples name Cairn 1.8.3 and a host binary 2.1.283 while this repository's VERSION reads 1.9.0, and it says docs/design-claims.md states that only one claim is tested where that document now says two. Are such facts refreshed to the current state in this milestone, or rewritten so the draft no longer states a fact that moves?
